report:
Your skepticism is justified: the claim that soursop/graviola “cures cancer in humans” is unsupported and should be treated as false as a medical claim. Soursop contains annonaceous acetogenins that can kill cancer cells in lab dishes and show effects in some animal models, but that is not evidence of benefit in people. Cancer Research UK says there is “not enough reliable evidence” that graviola works as a cancer treatment, despite internet promotion as a cure (https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/treatment/complementary-alternative-therapies/individual-therapies/graviola). Memorial Sloan Kettering likewise notes traditional use and lab interest, but emphasizes unclear translation of safety/efficacy to humans (https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/graviola).

Regulators have acted against cure claims: FDA warned a seller for asserting soursop was “10,000 times stronger” than chemotherapy (https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/warning-letters/amazing-sour-sop-inc-512798-04172017). There are also safety signals: annonacin exposure has been associated with atypical parkinsonism in Guadeloupe studies (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18816693/). Bottom line: do not replace surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or clinical trials with soursop; patients considering it should discuss risks and interactions with their oncology team.
